High Court Of Madhya Pradesh
 At Jabalpur
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: This is a petition seeking quashment of criminal proceedings instituted vide Crime No. 112/2014 for the offences under Sections 498-A, 506 Part-II/34 of I.P.C and Section 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act pending in R.C.T No. 5805731/2014 before the Judicial Magistrate First Class- Bhopal.
2. It is contended by the counsel that in the present case the parties have arrived at an amicable settlement and an application for compromise was filed before the Court below.
The Court below, so far as the offences, which were registered under Sections 506 I.P.C is concerned has allowed the said application and the applicants have been acquitted.

However, the Court below has not allowed the said application in respect of offence registered under Sections 498-A of I.P.C and Section 4 of Dowry Prohibition Act as the said offences are non-compoundable.
It is contended by the counsel that

before the Court below both the parties entered their appearance, they were identified by their counsel and the complainant also expressed before the Court that she will settle the dispute amicably without any coercion or threat.

It is thus, contended by the counsel that the present application for compounding the offences deserves to be allowed in view of the law laid down by the Apex Court in B.S. Joshi and others v. State of Haryana and another - (AIR 2003 SC 1386).

entities.text: B.S. Joshi and others v. State of Haryana and another - (AIR 2003 SC 1386)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
3. Counsel for the respondent No. 2 has supported the contention of the counsel and does not dispute that the parties have already arrived at an amicable settlement.
4.

Considering the aforesaid submissions, it is evident from the law laid down by the Apex Court in B.S. Joshi (supra) that Section 320, Cr. P.C. does not limit the powers of the High Court which are conferred by virtue 482 of Criminal Procedure Code of Section.

The Apex Court in the case of B.S.
Joshi (supra)

held in paragraphs 12 to 15 as under:
12.
The special features in such matrimonial matters are evident.
It becomes the duty of the Court to encourage genuine settlements of matrimonial disputes.

sentences.text: The observations made by this Court, though in a slightly different context, in G.V. Rao v. L.H.V. Prasad & Ors. [(2000) 3 SCC 693] are very apt for determining the approach required to be kept in view in matrimonial dispute by the courts, it was said that there has been an outburst of matrimonial disputes in recent times.

entities.text: G.V. Rao v. L.H.V. Prasad & Ors. [(2000) 3 SCC 693]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Marriage is a sacred ceremony, the main purpose of which is to enable the young couple to settle down in life and live peacefully.

But little matrimonial skirmishes suddenly erupt which often assume serious proportions resulting in commission of heinous crimes in which elders of the family are also involved with the result that those who could have counselled and brought about rapprochement are rendered helpless on their being arrayed as accused in the criminal case.

There are many other reasons which need not be mentioned here for not encouraging matrimonial litigation so that the parties may ponder over their defaults and terminate their disputes amicably by mutual agreement instead of fighting it out in a court of law where it takes years and years to conclude and in that process the parties lose their "young" days in chasing their "cases" in different courts.
14.
There is no doubt that the object of introducing Chapter XX-A containing Section 498A in the Indian Penal Code was to prevent the torture to a woman by her husband or by relatives of her husband.
Section 498A was added with a view to punishing a husband and his relatives who harass or torture the wife to coerce her or her relatives to satisfy unlawful demands of dowry.
The hyper-technical view would be counter productive and would act against interests of women and against the object for which this provision was added.
There is every likelihood that non-exercise of inherent power to quash the proceedings to meet the ends of justice would prevent women from settling earlier.
That is not the object of Chapter XXA of Indian Penal Code.

15. In view of the above discussion, we hold that the High Court in exercise of its inherent powers can quash criminal proceedings or FIR or complaint and Section 320 of the Code does not limit or affect the powers under Section 482 of the Code.

5. Thus, in view of the aforesaid as the parties have arrived at an amicable settlement and the complainant does not wish to continue with the prosecution against the present applicant, in the considered view of this Court, the proceedings instituted against the applicants deserves to be quashed.

6. Accordingly, all criminal proceedings instituted vide Crime No. 112/2014 for the offences under Sections 498-A, 506 Part-II/34 of I.P.C and Section 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act pending in R.C.T No. 5805731/2014 before the Judicial Magistrate First Class- Bhopal stands quashed in view of the compromise and the present applicants are acquitted of the aforesaid charges.
Their bail bonds, if any, be discharged.
7. The petition stands allowed.
